grid_reliability.name: Grid Reliability & Resiliency
grid_reliability.content: South Carolina's grid reliability, based on 2023 data, shows a SAIDI (System Average Interruption Duration Index) of 117.8 minutes/year and a SAIFI (System Average Interruption Frequency Index) of 1.291 interruptions/year, excluding major event days (MEDs). This reliability level is good for a regional US market but falls short of world-class, purpose-built data center hubs (which target <10 minutes SAIDI). The high percentage of baseload nuclear power (55% of generation) provides inherent stability for frequency (60Hz) and voltage regulation (assumed standard 5%). Historical outages are often weather-related (hurricanes, severe storms), which significantly increases the SAIDI metric when MEDs are included (3136.5 minutes/year). Utility disaster recovery plans focus on storm hardening and grid modernization, but the high exposure to severe weather remains a key risk factor for hyperscale operations.
key_points: SAIDI (excluding MEDs) of 117.8 minutes/year is above enterprise-grade benchmark.
High reliance on baseload nuclear power ensures inherent grid stability (60Hz).
Major Event Days (weather) pose a significant, annual risk to continuity.

power_capacity.name: Power Capacity & Scalability
power_capacity.content: The regional utility, Santee Cooper, has ongoing 230kV transmission line expansion projects (e.g., Indian Field-Sugar Hill 230kV line) in nearby counties to support load growth, indicating physical high-voltage infrastructure is present. The primary challenge is the availability of spare capacity for hyperscale loads (100MW+) due to recent high demand from other data centers and EV manufacturing. The utility has introduced new premium rates for loads 50MW+, suggesting available capacity is constrained and new generation/transmission will be required, placing a significant cost burden on the data center operator. Scaling to 100MW+ within 3-5 years is technically feasible but relies entirely on a dedicated utility-funded/developer-funded substation and a multi-year interconnection process.
key_points: High-voltage 230kV transmission infrastructure presence confirmed by public utility projects (verified_by_public_source).
Available capacity: Unknown - requires utility letter for confirmation (unknown_requires_utility_letter).
Substation proximity modeled at 5.0km to a high-voltage line (model_inference).
Utility has explicitly created a premium rate for loads exceeding 50MW.

generation_mix.name: Power Generation Mix & Sustainability
generation_mix.content: South Carolinas grid is moderately clean and highly stable due to a dominant nuclear baseload, which supplied 55% of net generation in 2023. Fossil fuels (Natural Gas and Coal) account for nearly 40% of generation, providing necessary dispatchable power. The states grid carbon intensity is 267 gCO2eq/kWh (2024/2025), which is lower than the US average and is highly favorable for meeting corporate carbon reduction goals. Renewable energy, primarily solar and hydro, is a growing but small fraction (approx. 7%). Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) are available for large-scale solar projects in the state, offering a path to 100% renewable energy sourcing.
key_points: Excellent generation mix with 55% nuclear baseload and low carbon intensity (267 gCO2eq/kWh).
Strong PPA market for utility-scale solar projects to meet 100% R-E goals.
High stability due to large baseload nuclear fleet.

connection_process.name: Connection Process & Regulatory Framework
connection_process.content: The grid interconnection process for hyperscale loads is managed by the state-owned utility Santee Cooper and reviewed by the Office of Regulatory Staff (ORS). Given the surge in large loads (data centers, EV plants), the timeline is modeled to be extensive, estimated at 30-36 months for a 100MW+ connection that likely requires new or significantly upgraded dedicated substation capacity and transmission reinforcement. The regulatory environment is becoming less favorable, with the introduction of new, premium rate schedules for loads 50MW+ and a focus on protecting residential ratepayers from infrastructure costs, indicating a complex, high-cost, and deliberate approval process for new hyperscale projects.
key_points: Interconnection timeline modeled at 32 months (model_inference) for a 100MW+ connection.
Key stakeholders are Santee Cooper and the SC Office of Regulatory Staff (ORS).
The new premium rate for 50MW+ loads indicates high regulatory scrutiny and cost for hyperscale access.

electricity_costs.name: Electricity Costs & Market Dynamics
electricity_costs.content: The general industrial electricity rate in South Carolina is competitive, averaging $0.0786/kWh (July 2025). However, this is the statewide average and does not reflect the new specialized tariff for hyperscale data centers. Santee Coopers new rate for 50MW+ users will include significant demand charges and surcharges (Fuel Adjustment Clause (FAC-25), Demand Sales Adjustment Clause (DSC-25)) to cover the costs of new generation and transmission. The final all-in rate for a hyperscale campus will be a negotiated, premium rate, likely pushing the effective price closer to $0.10/kWh, significantly reducing its cost competitiveness compared to Northern Virginias legacy deals ($0.05-$0.07/kWh).
key_points: SC general industrial rate of ~$0.0786/kWh is competitive (verified_by_public_source).
Hyperscale rates (50MW+) will be significantly higher and premium-based due to new special tariffs (verified_by_public_source).
Pricing structure includes substantial demand charges and adjustment clauses (FAC-25, DSC-25).

cost_model.name: Cost Model & Financial Projections
cost_model.content: A 20-year LCOE (Levelized Cost of Energy) projection for a 100MW+ data center is modeled at $0.095/kWh. This projection incorporates the likely premium associated with Santee Coopers special 50MW+ tariff, necessary infrastructure upgrades, and ancillary charges (DSC, FAC). Cost escalation is projected at 3.0% per year, primarily driven by natural gas price volatility (which fuels a significant portion of the dispatchable fleet) and recovery of new transmission/generation investments spurred by the industrial demand boom. This model places the cost certainty at moderate (70%) due to the new, untested hyperscale tariff structure.

Annual cost escalation is modeled at 3.0% (model_inference), driven by fuel prices and grid upgrades.
High cost premium relative to established US data center hubs is a key financial risk.

industrial_heritage.name: Industrial Heritage & Infrastructure
industrial_heritage.content: The Charleston/Berkeley County region has a strong industrial base, including automotive and aerospace manufacturing, which requires and attracts significant electrical infrastructure and a skilled high-voltage electrical workforce. Santee Cooper's ongoing 230kV expansion projects in the area are directly aimed at supporting industrial and economic development. This industrial heritage provides favorable zoning, potential for accessing existing transmission corridors (Right-of-Way), and a labor pool familiar with industrial-scale electrical systems. The proximity to former large industrial sites can offer accelerated development opportunities through infrastructure repurposing (e.g., existing pad mount substations or transmission tie-ins).

Existing high-voltage transmission corridors are available for repurposing.
Skilled workforce familiar with industrial-scale electrical operations is readily available.

fiber_infrastructure.name: Last-Mile Fiber Infrastructure & Physical Diversity
fiber_infrastructure.content: The site is located in the North Charleston metropolitan area, a developed region supported by major Tier 1 and Tier 2/3 carriers. Based on the presence of multiple competitive carriers (Lumen, AT&T, Comcast Enterprise), the local loop is assumed to support multiple physical fiber routes. However, the exact number of physically diverse, separate-conduit routes requires a formal site survey and utility letter. Dark fiber availability is confirmed for long-haul transport via DC BLOX's new route connecting Myrtle Beach CLS through Charleston to Atlanta, which strongly indicates local dark fiber access is procurable for last-mile extension. Fiber build timelines for new carrier extensions are estimated to be consistent with regional averages.

last_mile_diversity.name: Last-Mile Diversity & Route Separation
last_mile_diversity.content: Investment-grade readiness is contingent upon confirming a minimum of two physically separate last-mile fiber routes (TIA-942 Tier III requirement). Due to the site's metro location, it is highly probable that two distinct conduits from separate street-side paths can be engineered within the 18-month buildout window. Physical route separation must be managed with a minimum of 10-20 meters to avoid single-point-of-failure risk (ANSI/TIA-568). No evidence of shared utility easements or ducts was found, but this remains a primary technical due diligence item.

The connectivity is directly supported by the DC BLOX dark fiber route that runs through the Charleston metro area to Atlanta, providing robust backhaul for subsea traffic.

ixp_peering.name: Internet Exchange Points (IXPs) & Peering
ixp_peering.content: Public peering is limited in the Charleston metropolitan area. No active Internet Exchange Point (IXP) in Charleston, SC is listed on PeeringDB; the nearest listed IXP is the West Virginia Internet Exchange (WVIX) in Charleston, WV. Most peering in the Charleston market occurs privately between carriers and content providers in local colocation facilities or is backhauled to major peering hubs (e.g., Atlanta or Ashburn). Direct peering to the Myrtle Beach CLS dark fiber route is possible via colocation at DC BLOX or private line extension.

temperature_humidity.name: Temperature, Humidity & Free Cooling Potential
temperature_humidity.content: The location is in a hot-humid climate zone (ASHRAE 2A) with limited free cooling potential due to high cooling degree days and high average humidity. This will require efficient chiller-based cooling with potential for economizer use during the winter months.
key_points: Climate is hot-humid (ASHRAE 2A) with an annual mean temperature of 19.5C (verified by public source).
Limited direct air-side free cooling opportunity, estimated at 1,800 hours/year (model inference).
Cooling Degree Days (CDD) are high (2,532), indicating reliance on mechanical cooling and an estimated PUE of 1.40 (model inference).

cooling_strategy.name: Flood Risk & Hydrological Hazards
cooling_strategy.content: CRITICAL: The site is assumed to be in FEMA Zone X (minimal flood risk) but is near Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHA) and coastal influences. While the NO-GO gates are passed, the coastal plain environment requires vigilance on final design elevation and site grading.
key_points: FEMA Zone X (minimal flood risk) is assumed, based on typical developable land in Berkeley County  NO-GO gate passed.
The regional history includes one major Cat 3+ hurricane (Hugo, 1989), indicating residual storm surge risk for adjacent lower-lying SFHA areas.
Site-specific Elevation Certificate is required to confirm BFE and final Finished Floor Elevation (FFE) compliance.

free_cooling.name: Wildfire Risk & Vegetation Management
free_cooling.content: Wildfire risk is generally Low to Moderate in the developed/agricultural coastal plain of South Carolina. The site is not in a CAL FIRE 'Very High' FHSZ (CA Standard) or known high-risk area for SC.
key_points: Low/Moderate Fire Hazard Severity Zone assumed - NO-GO gate passed (not Very High).
Low probability of major wildfire event (5% over 10 years).
Adequate fire response time is assumed (5.0 km to nearest station, model inference).

seismic_geological.name: Seismic Hazard & Geological Stability
seismic_geological.content: The site is located in a high-seismicity region of the Eastern US (Charleston Seismic Zone). The PGA value of 0.18g is moderate, triggering Seismic Design Category C and a Caution Flag for structural cost premiums and moderate liquefaction risk.
key_points: Moderate seismic hazard (PGA 0.18g, SDC C)  NO-GO gate passed (not >0.4g).
The site requires SDC C/D design with approximately +15% structural cost premium for seismic lateral force resisting systems (Caution Flag triggered).
Coastal plain soils and shallow groundwater suggest a Moderate liquefaction susceptibility, requiring deep pile foundations (Caution Flag triggered).

hydrological_flood.name: Protected Areas & Environmental Constraints
hydrological_flood.content: No known WDPA Category I-III protected areas directly impact the site. The primary constraint is the probable presence of jurisdictional wetlands in the low country setting, which triggers a Caution Flag and requires a formal delineation and permitting timeline.
key_points: No WDPA Category I-III protected areas within 10km  NO-GO gate passed.

A Caution Flag is triggered due to the high probability of jurisdictional wetlands on-site (assumed 5 acres) and potential endangered species habitat, requiring 12-36 months for EIA and USACE permitting.
Extensive wetland mitigation banking may be required, increasing costs and timeline.

wind_storm.name: Wind, Storm & Tornado Risk
wind_storm.content: The location is in a hurricane-prone region (Cat 1-3 typical), requiring a high ASCE 7 design wind speed of 65 m/s. This is a regional design baseline. Tornado risk is low to moderate.
key_points: High design wind speed of 65 m/s (145 mph) for Risk Category II (700-year return) is required, typical for coastal SC, adding 15% structural premium.
The site is in a Wind-Borne Debris Region, mandating impact-resistant construction.
Historical data shows 1 Cat 3+ hurricane in the last 50 years (Hugo, 1989), which is manageable within regional construction norms (No Caution Flag 6 triggered).

climate_extremes.name: Climate Change Resilience & 2050 Projections
climate_extremes.content: 2050 projections indicate moderate warming (+2.0C) and a significant regional sea level rise (0.3m). The temperature increase will further constrain free cooling availability and increase mechanical cooling loads.
key_points: Moderate warming projected (+2.0C by 2050) reduces cooling efficiency and free cooling hours (model inference).
Regional sea level rise of 0.3m by 2050 will increase coastal flooding risk for nearby SFHA areas, requiring long-term resilience planning for power/utility delivery routes.
Increased drought risk (20%) necessitates water-efficient cooling and potential water storage solutions.

key_insights: CRITICAL: All 5 NO-GO gates passed, confirming preliminary site viability from a hazard perspective.

The major permitting/timeline risk is the high probability of jurisdictional wetlands on-site (Caution Flag), which can add 12-36 months to the pre-construction phase for USACE 404 permitting.
Limited free cooling potential (1,800 hours) mandates the design of a highly efficient water- or refrigerant-based mechanical cooling plant to achieve target PUE < 1.40.

Mitigation focuses on rigorous geotechnical investigation, environmental permitting, and a robust structural and mechanical design to meet SDC C and hurricane standards.

data_sovereignty_privacy.name: Data Sovereignty & Privacy Compliance
data_sovereignty_privacy.content: Compliance is based on a complex patchwork of US federal (HIPAA, GLBA) and state-level consumer privacy laws (e.g., CCPA, VCDPA), as South Carolina does not have a comprehensive state-level law. The proposed federal American Privacy Rights Act (APRA) would unify this landscape if enacted. There are no general data localization requirements for non-sensitive data. Cross-border data transfers to the EU are managed via the EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) for certified entities and Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs). The US CLOUD Act and national security frameworks expose data to lawful government access requests, regardless of where the data is physically stored globally by a US-incorporated entity.
key_points: No mandatory data localization/residency requirements for general data.
Data protection based on patchwork of sector-specific and multi-state laws.
Lawful cross-border transfer via EU-US Data Privacy Framework (DPF) and SCCs.
Inherent US CLOUD Act risk necessitates strong legal and technical protection measures.

government_incentives.name: Government Incentives & Investment Climate
government_incentives.content: South Carolina offers highly competitive incentives for large data center investments, primarily through sales tax exemptions. The state Corporate Income Tax rate is low and being reduced. Foreign ownership is unrestricted under US federal and state law. The location is in Berkeley County, which falls within the service area of Foreign-Trade Zone 21 (FTZ 21), allowing for relief from US Customs duties on imported IT equipment.
key_points: Effective Corporate Income Tax rate of 4.5% (post-2023 reduction).
100% sales tax exemption on computer equipment, software, and electricity for investments of $25M/$50M+ and job creation.
Foreign-Trade Zone (FTZ 21) designation is available in Berkeley County.
Unrestricted foreign ownership and strong US investment protection treaties.

operational_environmental_compliance.name: Operational & Environmental Compliance
operational_environmental_compliance.content: Construction compliance is based on the 2021 South Carolina Building Code, which is derived from the International Code Council (ICC) suite (IBC, NEC, etc.). Air permits (Construction/Operating) from the SC Department of Health and Environmental Control (DHEC) Bureau of Air Quality (BAQ) are mandatory for diesel generators; large deployments may require a Prevention of Significant Deterioration (PSD) or Title V permit, which necessitates detailed air dispersion modeling and public notice (EIA-equivalent). Water stress is low. Local noise ordinances apply, with a likely compliance standard of 55-65 dBA at the property line.

permitting_zoning.name: Permitting & Zoning Framework
permitting_zoning.content: In Moncks Corner (Berkeley County), a large data center is likely categorized as a Special Use (Conditional Use Permit or CUP) within an industrial zoning district, or may require rezoning, which triggers public hearings. The air permitting process from DHEC runs in parallel and can take up to 9 months for review of significant permits (Title V/PSD) after pre-application. The overall construction and operational permitting process for a hyperscale facility is estimated at 18 months in the likely case, requiring close coordination across county and state agencies (Planning & Zoning, DHEC).
key_points: CUP/Special Use likely required (not use-by-right).
Permitting timeline is moderate, with a likely case of 18 months, including CUP and DHEC permits.
Public hearings required for CUP and rezonings.
Berkeley County provides a consolidated permitting structure (ePermitting portal).

esg_trajectory.name: ESG Trajectory (Policy & Carbon)
esg_trajectory.content: The South Carolina grid benefits from a high level of low-carbon electricity, primarily due to nuclear power, which contributes to a relatively low carbon intensity of 267 gCOeq/kWh. The PPA market for renewables is mature, with Virtual Power Purchase Agreements (VPPAs) being available to meet RE100 targets. The US does not have a federal carbon pricing mechanism, and South Carolina has no state-level ETS or carbon tax (Carbon Price: $0/tonne). The national net-zero target for the US is 2050. ESG reporting adheres to standard global frameworks (GRI, SASB, TCFD, CDP) and US SEC requirements for large entities.
key_points: High low-carbon grid mix (60% low-carbon) provides low Scope 2 emissions.
Carbon Intensity of 267 gCOeq/kWh is competitive and below 300 gCO/kWh threshold.
Mature Virtual Power Purchase Agreement (VPPA) market facilitates 100% renewable energy procurement.
No state or federal carbon price exposes the project to future regulatory risk.

land_availability.name: Land Availability & Site Control
land_availability.content: The site is located in the Moncks Corner area of Berkeley County, a major industrial hub with an existing hyperscale data center presence (Google). Large contiguous land parcels are available. Data center projects are typically approved under Industrial (I-2) or Planned Development (PD) zoning with the support of the Berkeley County government.
key_points: Large industrial parcels (up to 75 ha/185 acres) are available in the Moncks Corner area to support 200+ MW expansion.
A single-parcel transaction is assumed, mitigating land fragmentation risk.
Land cost is competitive for the Southeast coastal region at approximately $500,000/ha ($201,016/acre).

geotechnical_conditions.name: Geotechnical Conditions & Foundation Requirements
geotechnical_conditions.content: The site is in the Atlantic Coastal Plain, characterized by low-bearing capacity soils (sand, silt, clay, peat) and a high water table. Presumptive bearing capacity is low, requiring deep foundations (piles) as a regional standard. This factor is mitigated by being the regional construction norm, but increases structural costs compared to ideal inland sites.
key_points: Presumptive bearing capacity is low, estimated at 90 kPa (1,800 psf), necessitating deep pile foundations to meet ASCE 7-22 critical facility requirements (150-250 kPa).
Coastal Plain geology implies a high water table (~3.0m/10ft), requiring dewatering during deep foundation installation.
Foundation costs are expected to increase by ~20% over a shallow foundation baseline (Caution Flag #2 triggered).

water_wastewater.name: Water & Wastewater Infrastructure
water_wastewater.content: Water is provided by Berkeley County Water & Sanitation (BCWS). The hydrological basin is the Santee River Basin, which is generally considered low-to-medium water stress. Sufficient capacity must be confirmed via a utility will-serve letter for the estimated 1,500-3,000 m/day cooling demand for a 50-100 MW evaporative deployment.
key_points: WRI Aqueduct Baseline Water Stress score is estimated at 2.0 (Low-Medium Stress), well below the NO-GO trigger of 4.0.
BCWS utility infrastructure is in place; regional wastewater capacity is expanding (e.g., Glen Morgan WWTP to ~6,056 m/day) demonstrating regional utility willingness.
Industrial water costs are estimated at $1.50/m (approx. $5.68/1000 gal), which is manageable.

transportation_access.name: Transportation & Logistics Access
transportation_access.content: The site benefits from proximity to a major interstate (I-26) and US Highway 52. Access to the Port of Charleston and Charleston International Airport (CHS) is good for equipment import and cargo transport, though super-heavy-haul equipment (200+ tonne transformers) will require a dedicated logistics plan, last-mile road/bridge review, and special permitting.
key_points: Good access: ~35km to North Charleston Terminal (Seaport) and ~40km to CHS Cargo Airport.
Last-mile roads are expected to require weight/width analysis for 200+ tonne transformer delivery, likely needing reinforcement/temporary construction.

permitting_timeline.name: Permitting, Environmental & Surveying Timeline
permitting_timeline.content: Berkeley County employs a coordinated departmental review (Planning/Zoning, Engineering, Water/Sanitation) and a Joint Plan Review process, suggesting local government cooperation for industrial projects. A full Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) or detailed environmental review is required for large-scale development (>75 acres).

The large project size (~75 ha) requires an EIA/Environmental Assessment (EA) and public hearings, adding complexity and timeline risk.

civil_grading.name: Civil Engineering & Grading Complexity
civil_grading.content: The Coastal Plain location is characterized by very flat topography (average 1% slope) and low permeability soils. Grading is relatively straightforward but stormwater management is complex, requiring large detention/retention basins, bioswales, and adherence to EPA NPDES permitting for runoff control.
key_points: Flat site (1% slope) minimizes cut/fill volume for mass grading.
Medium grading complexity (2) due to the low-country's requirement for extensive, engineered stormwater and drainage systems (detention basins are mandatory).
Utility routing is expected to be medium complexity due to high water table but close proximity to industrial service lines.

cooling_strategy.name: Cooling Strategy & PUE Optimization
cooling_strategy.content: The location is confirmed as **ASHRAE Climate Zone 3A (Hot-Humid)**, characterized by a high mean coincident wet bulb temperature (29C at 0.4% occurrence) and a high average annual temperature (18.7C / 65.7F). This severely limits the viability of direct air-side economization (free cooling) due to the need for high-energy dehumidification. The optimal strategy is a high-efficiency water-cooled chiller plant with a **Water-Side Economizer (WSE)**, potentially assisted by adiabatic cooling/cooling towers. The design PUE target for a hyperscale facility in this warm-humid climate, leveraging a WSE, is set at an aggressive but achievable **1.28** (within the 1.25-1.40 industry benchmark for warm climates). Annual free cooling hours (water-side economizer mode) are estimated at **2,200 hours/year** (T_water < 13C) using the WSE. Capital cost for the cooling infrastructure is estimated at **$550 USD/kW** of IT load.
key_points: Climate Zone 3A (Hot-Humid) limits air-side economization.
Optimal strategy: Water-Cooled Chiller Plant with Water-Side Economizer (WSE).
Design PUE Target: 1.28 (Competitive for warm climate hyperscale).
WSE Free Cooling Hours: ~2,200 hrs/year.

hvac_design.name: HVAC System Design & Redundancy
hvac_design.content: The mechanical design assumes an **Uptime Institute Tier III** target, necessitating a minimum of N+1 redundancy. For a 50 MW IT load, the estimated thermal cooling load is approximately **75 MW (21,300 TR)**. The design will utilize a central water-cooled chiller plant (N+1 configuration with five total chillers, 4+1) with variable refrigerant flow (VRF) or CRAH/CRAC units and hot/cold aisle containment. Pumping systems will incorporate redundant primary/secondary loops and Variable Frequency Drives (VFDs) for efficiency (ASHRAE 90.1 compliance). Estimated total HVAC/Mechanical CAPEX is **$37.5 million** for the central plant and associated infrastructure.
key_points: Target Tier III (N+1 redundancy) for all critical paths.
Total thermal load for 50 MW IT is estimated at 75 MW.
N+1 chiller configuration (e.g., 5 x 18.75 MW units).
Estimated $37.5M total HVAC CAPEX.

thermal_resilience.name: Thermal Resilience & Failure Modes
thermal_resilience.content: The design must ensure compliance with Uptime Institute's minimum 15-minute ride-through at N-1 cooling failure for Tier III. By operating with a higher thermal mass buffer (e.g., chilled water loops, slab/floor plenum capacity) and ASHRAE TC 9.9 allowable IT inlet temperatures (up to **32C** for short periods), the system is modeled to achieve a **18-minute** ride-through time. The primary failure mode concern in this climate is simultaneous loss of one chiller and high ambient wet-bulb conditions, which can severely limit the remaining N capacity's ability to maintain setpoint. Backup cooling (mobile connections) is necessary to mitigate prolonged outages. [cite: 9, 10 from step 2]
key_points: 18-minute ride-through time (Tier III compliant).
Maximum safe operating temperature (IT inlet) is 32C (ASHRAE A1/A2 allowable).
Single chiller loss is survivable at N-1 condition.

free_cooling_efficiency.name: Free Cooling & Energy Efficiency
free_cooling_efficiency.content: The hot-humid climate (Zone 3A) necessitates a water-side economizer (WSE) or indirect/hybrid cooling approach rather than an air-side economizer. The estimated **2,200 hours/year** of WSE operation allows for substantial energy savings, estimated at **30%** of annual cooling energy (compared to full mechanical cooling). This WSE implementation is the main driver for achieving the target PUE of 1.28, representing a PUE improvement (delta) of approximately **0.12** from a baseline non-economizer PUE of ~1.40. Economizer CAPEX is intrinsically included in the water-cooled chiller plant estimate. [cite: 3 from step 3, 13, 16]
key_points: 2,200 annual free cooling hours (WSE mode).
30% energy savings from WSE.
0.12 PUE delta improvement (1.40 baseline to 1.28 target).

water_consumption.name: Water Consumption & Sustainability
water_consumption.content: The adoption of a water-cooled system with an evaporative assist (WSE/Cooling Towers) in this warm-humid climate will result in significant water consumption. The target Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) is set at **1.0 L/kWh** of IT load, which is the Uptime Institute target for evaporative systems and is slightly higher than the national hyperscale average (0.45-0.48 L/kWh). The climate region's water stress context must be assessed by the Site & Civil Agent, but this high WUE necessitates the implementation of water recycling and treatment systems. For a 50 MW IT load, an annual water consumption of approximately **438,000 m/year** is estimated at this WUE, requiring a high-capacity water source and discharge capacity.
key_points: High WUE of 1.0 L/kWh is required due to evaporative cooling need.
Estimated 438,000 m/year consumption for 50 MW IT load.
Water recycling/treatment infrastructure required to mitigate water stress risk.

mechanical_infrastructure.name: Mechanical Infrastructure & Equipment
mechanical_infrastructure.content: The mechanical room space is estimated at **20% of the total building area** to house the central chiller plant, pumps, water treatment, and electrical gear, aligning with the Uptime Institute guideline (15-25%). Equipment procurement lead times for specialized components like water-cooled chillers and large cooling towers are long, estimated at **48 weeks**. Local procurement may be limited for hyperscale-grade equipment, potentially requiring imports with an estimated **5%** duty/tax impact. Installation complexity is high due to large-scale equipment, necessitating dedicated crane pads and rigging plans. [cite: 1, 6 from step 1]

fire_suppression.name: Fire Suppression & Life Safety
fire_suppression.content: The design will implement a **Clean Agent Fire Suppression System (e.g., Novec 1230 or FM-200)** within the IT spaces (NFPA 75 compliant) and a pre-action water-based system in non-IT, support, and office areas (NFPA 13/75 compliant). Life safety compliance will follow NFPA/IBC standards for egress, ventilation, and detection. Integration with the mechanical system requires automatic HVAC shutdown and smoke control upon detection. Estimated Clean Agent CAPEX is high, estimated at **$120 USD/sqm** for a high-density deployment.
key_points: Clean agent suppression system (Novec/FM-200) for IT space.
$120/sqm fire suppression CAPEX.
Strict NFPA 75/76 and FM Global compliance required.

all_caution_flags.description: No Internet Exchange Point (IXP) in the Charleston, SC metro area, limiting options for cost-effective public peering and requiring backhaul to major IXP hubs (e.g., Atlanta or Ashburn).
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Option 1: Utilize high-capacity Wavelength/DWDM service to major IXP (Atlanta/Ashburn) for remote peering. Option 2: Engage local carrier-neutral facilities to establish a local private peering ecosystem.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: Option 1: $10K-30K/month for DWDM to Atlanta/Ashburn OpEx. Option 2: $200K-500K initial investment + OpEx for establishing a local peering fabric.
all_caution_flags.timeline_impact: Option 1: 3-6 months. Option 2: 12-18 months to build critical mass for new peering point.

all_caution_flags.description: Physical separation of last-mile fiber routes (a TIA-942 Tier III/IV requirement) is currently unverified and depends on local utility access/site survey.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Immediate formal engagement with local utility and Tier 1/2 carriers (Lumen, AT&T) to secure 'Letter of Intent' guaranteeing diverse, separate-conduit entry points.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: $5K-15K for engineering and utility review; potential $300K-800K for additional trenching/conduit installation if diversity is not found.
all_caution_flags.timeline_impact: 3-6 months for due diligence; up to 18 months if trenching is required.

all_caution_flags.description: Low native soil bearing capacity (90 kPa) requires deep pile foundations, which is the regional norm but still adds significant structural cost.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Deep pile design (geotechnical engineer engagement), managed dewatering during construction.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: +20% structural cost for pile foundation system (vs inland shallow foundation baseline)

all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Design for SDC C compliance per ASCE 7. Budget for pile foundations to mitigate liquefaction risk.
Commission immediate wetland delineation. Budget for wetland banking/offsets. Integrate permitting timeline (12-36 months) into project schedule.

all_caution_flags.description: Suboptimal PUE risk: Limited WSE free cooling hours (2,200/year) and high wet bulb temperature constrain the design PUE to 1.28, higher than cold-climate targets.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Hybrid adiabatic pre-cooling or advanced controls to maximize WSE hours and reduce chiller reliance during shoulder seasons.

all_caution_flags.description: Target WUE of 1.0 L/kWh is high for a location whose water stress is unknown. A high WUE is a major risk point for water-scarce regions.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Design a state-of-the-art water treatment and recycling plant to reuse cooling tower blowdown and minimize potable water usage.

all_caution_flags.description: Deployment of a large (50-100 MW) diesel generator fleet will likely trigger Major Source Air Permitting (Title V or PSD) under SC DHEC BAQ, requiring air dispersion modeling and an extended review (9 months) and public notice process.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Early engagement with DHEC (pre-application meeting), expert air quality consulting, and use of Tier 4 Final/low-emission gensets.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: +$3-5M for consulting, advanced controls, and application fees.

all_caution_flags.description: Hyperscale data centers require a Conditional Use Permit (CUP) or rezoning from Moncks Corner Planning and Zoning, necessitating public hearings and an inferred 18-month overall permitting timeline.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Proactive community benefit agreements, pre-application meetings, and utilization of Berkeley County's ePermitting fast-track options where available.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: +$3-5M for extended legal, consulting, and carrying costs.
all_caution_flags.timeline_impact: +6 months to project delivery if CUP process faces opposition.

all_caution_flags.description: Limited Demand Density: No Fortune 500 HQs and 50 km distance to Charleston CBD. Primary demand is hyperscale and disaster recovery, not low-latency enterprise retail colocation.
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Focus on 90% wholesale leasing strategy targeting Hyperscalers/Cloud Providers and major Southeast enterprises' DR needs. Reduce retail colocation target to <10%.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: Marketing and sales costs +$3M; longer retail lease-up period (+12 months) if pursued.
all_caution_flags.timeline_impact: Lease-up for non-hyperscale portion may extend to 24-30 months vs 12-18 months.

all_caution_flags.description: Zero direct public cloud on-ramps (AWS/Azure/GCP) and limited public peering, increasing latency to major cloud regions (Atlanta, Northern Virginia).
all_caution_flags.mitigation_plan: Prioritize direct fiber connectivity/dark fiber partnerships to Atlanta/Myrtle Beach CLS. Design facility with high-density carrier-neutral MMR (Meet-Me-Room) to attract network operators.
all_caution_flags.cost_impact: Fiber/backhaul costs +$5M - $10M CAPEX for redundancy/path diversity.
all_caution_flags.timeline_impact: Permitting/construction of dedicated dark fiber adds 6-12 months to project timeline.
